text: March, eighteen ninety-four. Pelican Valley, deep in Yellowstone's backcountry. The snow is shoulder high, and an Army scout named Felix Burgess is following a trail of snowshoe tracks.
At the end of the trail, he finds a man bent over a dead bison, knife in hand. His rifle is leaning out of reach.
The man is Ed Howell, the most notorious poacher in the park. He's been killing Yellowstone's last wild bison for their heads. And when he sees the scout, he throws up his hands.
This is the real photograph, taken after his capture. Howell had killed at least eleven bison that winter. At the time, there was almost no law to punish him for it.

Within two months, that would change. And the reason it changed is one of the strangest chapters in the history of America's parks: for thirty-two years, Yellowstone was run by the United States Army.
It started with pictures. In eighteen seventy-one, a government survey led by Ferdinand Hayden explored Yellowstone. With it came a photographer, William Henry Jackson, and a painter, Thomas Moran.

Jackson hauled a huge camera, glass plates and a portable darkroom on mules, developing every image on the spot, sometimes minutes after he took it. Moran sketched in watercolor, then went home and painted the canyon on a canvas seven feet tall. Congress later bought that painting for ten thousand dollars, an enormous sum at the time.

Most members of Congress had never seen the West. Jackson's photographs and Moran's paintings showed them a place that looked unreal: boiling springs, a golden canyon, waterfalls. On March first, eighteen seventy-two, President Ulysses S. Grant signed a law making Yellowstone the world's first national park, as the idea is understood today.

You may have heard how the idea was born. In eighteen seventy, explorers sat around a campfire right here, at the meeting of two rivers, and one of them proposed that the land should belong to everyone. It's a great story. It probably never happened. About twenty firsthand accounts of that expedition survive, and not one of them mentions it. The story first appeared in print thirty-five years later.

What did happen is less romantic. Congress created the park, and then gave it almost nothing. The first superintendent, Nathaniel Langford, wasn't paid at all. In five years, he went into the park twice. Once with the survey, and once to throw out a squatter.

So people did whatever they wanted. Hunters slaughtered elk by the thousands for their hides. Tourists broke off pieces of geyser cones as souvenirs, carved their names into the rock, and threw logs and junk into geysers just to see what would happen.

In eighteen seventy-seven, a new superintendent, [Philetus](/fɪlˈiːtəs/) Norris, finally got a salary and some money. He built a log blockhouse headquarters on a hill above Mammoth, and he built roads. Parts of his route still form the Grand Loop you drive today. He hired a tough mountain man named Harry [Yount](/jˈaʊnt/) as the park's first gamekeeper, often called the first park ranger.
But Norris had no real power to arrest anyone. There was no law to enforce. And in eighteen eighty-six, Congress cut off the money entirely.
With no one left to protect the park, the Secretary of the Interior did the only thing he could. He asked the Army for help.

On August seventeenth, eighteen eighty-six, Captain Moses Harris rode into Mammoth with fifty men of the First U.S. Cavalry. His new office was a broken-down blacksmith shop. One early park historian, Hiram Chittenden, later described Harris as "vigorous and uncompromising in suppressing lawlessness."
Harris didn't waste time. He threw out rule-breakers, stopped cattle from grazing near the geysers, and posted soldiers at the most famous sights.

A couple of years later, fifteen infantry soldiers were stationed at Old Faithful. Besides guarding it, they started explaining the geysers to visitors. Park historians say those talks were the beginning of what rangers still do today. They became known as the Immortal Fifteen.
Think about that the next time a ranger explains a geyser to you. The first people to do it in Yellowstone were soldiers.

The Army was supposed to be temporary. It stayed for thirty-two years. Its camp at the foot of the terraces became a real fort, Fort Yellowstone. By nineteen ten, more than three hundred soldiers lived here.
Thirty-five of the fort's buildings are still standing, and they're still the park's headquarters. If you've ever driven through Mammoth, you've driven through an old cavalry post.

Soldiers lived in small stations across the park, sixteen of them by the end. In summer they patrolled on horseback. In winter, they patrolled on skis, alone or in pairs, for days at a time, sleeping in small backcountry cabins and hunting for poachers' tracks in the snow. Civilian Army scouts went with them. Some of their diaries still survive in the park's archives.

In eighteen ninety-six, a unit of Black soldiers from the twenty-fifth Infantry, the famous Buffalo Soldiers, even rode bicycles through the park, testing whether bikes could replace horses. They posed for a photograph on the terraces at Mammoth.
Which brings us back to Ed Howell, hands in the air in Pelican Valley.

By luck, a writer named Emerson Hough was in the park that winter, traveling with the official park photographer, F. Jay Haynes. Hough sent word of the capture to his editor, George Bird Grinnell, at the magazine Forest and Stream.

Grinnell was one of the most powerful conservationists in the country. With his friend Theodore Roosevelt, he had founded the Boone and Crockett Club. The magazine ran the story with photographs, and the outrage spread fast.

There's a twist here. According to Smithsonian librarians, the gruesome photos of dead bison that ran with the story weren't Howell's kills at all. They were older images from another hunt. But the point landed.

On May seventh, eighteen ninety-four, a new law was approved to protect the animals of Yellowstone. Hunting was banned. Poachers could be fined up to a thousand dollars and jailed for two years. Their guns, horses and traps could be taken. The commander of the park called it "the most fortunate thing that ever happened to the park."
The law came too late to really punish Howell. But it was written because of him.
Even with the new law, the herd almost didn't make it. By nineteen-oh-two, only twenty-three wild bison were left in the park.
The soldiers had other problems too. By the early nineteen-hundreds, tourists toured the park in long lines of stagecoaches. And stagecoaches full of wealthy travelers attracted robbers.

On August twenty-fourth, nineteen-oh-eight, near Kepler Cascades on the road between Old Faithful and West Thumb, a single masked man stepped out of the trees. One by one, he stopped the coaches as they came around the bend. By the most-cited count, he robbed seventeen of them, more than a hundred and seventy passengers. He was never caught.

Six years later, in nineteen fourteen, it happened again near Shoshone Point. This time, one passenger took out his camera and photographed the robber in the middle of the hold-up. Another coach quietly turned around and raced back to raise the alarm. The passenger's picture, along with witness testimony, helped convict a man named Ed Trafton, although historians still debate whether he was really the robber.

In nineteen-oh-three, Theodore Roosevelt laid the cornerstone of this arch at the park's north entrance. Its inscription reads: "For the benefit and enjoyment of the people." During that visit, the President camped in the park, and soldiers from Fort Yellowstone guarded his camp near Tower Fall.

But the Army never wanted to be a park service forever. In nineteen sixteen, Congress created the National Park Service. Some of the soldiers who loved Yellowstone took off their uniforms and stayed on as the first park rangers.
It didn't go smoothly. The troops came back in nineteen seventeen. Then, on October thirty-first, nineteen eighteen, the last soldiers marched out of Fort Yellowstone for good.
They left something behind. The ranger's famous flat hat traces its roots to the wide-brimmed hats of the cavalry who rode in back in eighteen eighty-six.
So the Army saved Yellowstone from people. But there's one more part of this story that the early park leaders liked to leave out.
Superintendent Norris claimed that Native people were afraid of the geysers and stayed away. The Park Service says the evidence shows the opposite. Tribes had known this land for thousands of years.

And in the summer of eighteen seventy-seven, just five years after the park was created, about eight hundred [Nez Perce](/nˌɛz pˈɜɹs/) men, women and children crossed Yellowstone, running from the U.S. Army. That's the next chapter. See you there.
